backlog.title: AI-Defined Vehicles Push Compute, Memory, And Validation Limits
backlog.summary:
The shift from software-defined to AI-defined vehicles raises questions about whether the hardware can keep up. 
The post AI-Defined Vehicles Push Compute, Memory, And Validation Limits appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.
bullets: The automotive industry is transitioning from software-defined to AI-defined vehicles, a shift projected to tap into a $1 trillion-plus market for physical AI over the next decade.
AI-defined vehicles require a fundamental architectural overhaul to handle increased compute, memory, and power demands, moving beyond static software updates to real-time, adaptive decision-making.

Semiconductor companies stand to gain new revenue streams as automakers demand specialized AI accelerators and advanced development tools to support both consumer-facing features and backend diagnostics.
The transition necessitates new methodologies for testing and validating complex, adaptable systems that must maintain reliability under harsh, real-world automotive operating conditions.

backlog.title: The Hidden Challenges of Edge AI Design
backlog.summary:
As models evolve faster than silicon cycles, chip architects must balance flexible compute, data movement, and defense-in-depth security.
The post The Hidden Challenges of Edge AI Design appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.
bullets: Chip architects are shifting focus from peak NPU TOPS to system-level metrics like memory bandwidth, latency, and power efficiency to accommodate evolving AI models.
The convergence of CPU, GPU, and NPU architectures is creating more heterogeneous designs to hedge against future workload shifts.
Security is becoming a primary design constraint, requiring hardware-level protection for models, data, and firmware from the initial architectural phase.

backlog.title: How smaller, distributed batteries could help the grid
backlog.summary: If you want to install a big battery in New York City, you have to cut through a notoriously tough tangle of regulations. That’s made it difficult to get large energy storage projects on the grid. Faced with those obstacles, some startups are getting creative, finding ways to use relatively small batteries in unexpected places,…
bullets: Startups are circumventing the regulatory and safety challenges associated with large-scale, centralized battery installations in dense urban environments like New York City.
Companies like PopWheels are deploying battery-swapping infrastructure for e-bikes and food carts, effectively replacing gas generators and reducing operational costs for small businesses.

Innovative consumer appliances, such as induction stoves with integrated batteries, are being marketed to provide both energy resilience and cost savings by avoiding expensive electrical panel upgrades.

Distributed energy storage models shift the value proposition of batteries from abstract grid benefits to concrete, user-facing utility, potentially accelerating the adoption of decentralized power solutions.

backlog.title: Don’t be fooled—LLMs don’t reason
backlog.summary: On an afternoon in Seoul in March 2016, I watched a program I helped build put a stone on the fifth line of a Go board in what looked like a gift to its human opponent. Move 37 in game two of the five-game match looked so absurd that some commentators thought it was a…
bullets: Former DeepMind researcher Thore Graepel argues that modern LLMs lack the 'search-based' reasoning machinery that allowed AlphaGo to achieve creative, non-intuitive breakthroughs.

AlphaGo’s success relied on a dual-system architecture that combined intuitive pattern recognition with a search tree to evaluate future consequences, a capability absent in current generative models.
The author contends that achieving trustworthy results in high-stakes fields like medicine requires moving beyond probabilistic text prediction toward explicit, tree-based reasoning architectures.

backlog.title: X-energy and its helium-cooled nuclear reactors
backlog.summary: X-energy is developing small modular reactors to satisfy some of the planet’s most power-hungry users: industrial manufacturers that need high temperatures to produce billions of tons of concrete, plastics, fibers, and chemicals. Solar panels and wind turbines are great at producing electricity but what heavy industry also needs is raw heat—and lots of it. The manufacture…
bullets: X-energy is developing small modular reactors (SMRs) that use helium gas as a coolant, allowing for operating temperatures high enough to decarbonize heavy industries like steel and chemical manufacturing.
The Xe-100 reactor utilizes TRISO fuel pebbles, which are designed to be corrosion-resistant and inherently safe against meltdowns during power loss.
By co-locating these reactors at industrial sites, the company aims to address the 18% of global greenhouse-gas emissions currently generated by high-temperature industrial heating.

backlog.title: Energy Dome and its carbon dioxide batteries
backlog.summary: There’s a growing need for long-duration storage to meet energy demand and balance out renewables on the grid. Energy Dome uses compressed carbon dioxide gas in its massive grid batteries, which can deliver power for up to 24 hours.  As the world races to meet growing electricity demand, solar and onshore wind power have become…
bullets: Energy Dome uses compressed carbon dioxide in a closed-loop system to provide long-duration energy storage, offering a scalable alternative to lithium-ion for grid balancing.
The system stores energy by compressing CO2 into a liquid state and releases it through a turbine to generate electricity when needed, with a capacity of up to 24 hours.
Following the launch of its first commercial plant in Sardinia in 2025, the company is planning 30 gigawatt-hours of projects across five continents.

backlog.title: Crossing Chiplet Boundaries With PCIe Over UCIe

The post Crossing Chiplet Boundaries With PCIe Over UCIe appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.

Verification frameworks must now be protocol-aware to ensure that PCIe transaction semantics remain intact when traversing the die-to-die interconnect.

The emergence of this technology highlights a growing tension between scientific progress in brain-computer interfaces and the urgent need for new frameworks to protect cognitive liberty.

backlog.title: Apple and a Hacker’s Future

Apple has released patches for macOS Tahoe, Sequoia, and Sonoma following the disclosure of the exploit at the Black Hat security conference.
The incident highlights the critical importance of restricting agent access and maintaining constrained environments for AI-driven workflows to mitigate the impact of system-level compromises.

backlog.title: Row-Parallel DRAM Computing Cuts Data-Reorganization Overhead (Syracuse, FAU, TU Dresden)
backlog.summary:
Researchers at Syracuse University, Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg, and TU Dresden published a technical paper titled “RAPID: Row-Parallel Arithmetic Processing in DRAM.” Abstract Excerpt: “Processing-using-memory (PUM) architectures perform computation directly within DRAM to reduce costly data movement between memory and processors. Because charge-sharing operations are confined to individual bitlines, existing DRAM-PUM architectures reorganize data into column-oriented, bit-serial... » read more
The post Row-Parallel DRAM Computing Cuts Data-Reorganization Overhead (Syracuse, FAU, TU Dresden) appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.
bullets: The RAPID architecture introduces row-parallel arithmetic processing within DRAM to eliminate the costly data-reorganization overhead typical of existing processing-using-memory (PUM) designs.
By adding migration and inversion cells to DRAM subarrays, the system enables horizontal data movement and logical operations without converting data to bit-serial formats.
This approach preserves CPU-compatible, word-parallel layouts, allowing for more efficient integration of in-memory computing with conventional processor architectures.

backlog.title: Backside Clock Meshes Cut Skew and Power in 2nm Nanosheets (UCSC)
backlog.summary:
Researchers at the University of California, Santa Cruz published a technical paper titled “Design Space Exploration of Backside Clock Meshes for 2 nm GAAFET BSPDN Technology.” Abstract Excerpt: “Clock meshes are used in high-performance VLSI designs to minimize skew and tolerate on-chip variation, but they spend scarce routing resources on premium metal layers. Backside power... » read more
The post Backside Clock Meshes Cut Skew and Power in 2nm Nanosheets (UCSC) appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.
bullets: Researchers at UCSC have performed the first design-space exploration of backside clock meshes specifically for 2nm GAAFET nanosheet technology.
By utilizing backside power delivery networks, designers can implement thick, low-resistance metal layers to reduce clock skew and power consumption.
The study highlights the architectural challenge of connecting backside meshes to frontside flip-flops, which necessitates the use of through-silicon vias (TSVs).

backlog.title: Monolithic 3D Memristor-TFT Stack For Programmable Neuromorphic Computing (SNU, Yonsei)
backlog.summary:
Researchers at Seoul National University and Yonsei University published a technical paper titled “Monolithic three-dimensionally integrated memristor-thin-film transistor for electrically programmable multimode reservoir computing.” Abstract Excerpt: “Reservoir computing offers an efficient framework for processing temporal information, but most hardware reservoirs exhibit fixed or narrowly tunable dynamics determined by intrinsic material relaxation time. A monolithically integrated... » read more
The post Monolithic 3D Memristor-TFT Stack For Programmable Neuromorphic Computing (SNU, Yonsei) appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.
bullets: Researchers have demonstrated a monolithically integrated memristor-TFT stack that enables electrically programmable temporal dynamics for reservoir computing.
By vertically integrating Ru/HfO2/TiN memristors with In2O3 channel TFTs, the system overcomes the fixed dynamics typically found in hardware-based neural reservoirs.
This 3D integration approach provides a more flexible framework for processing temporal information, which is essential for advanced neuromorphic computing applications.

backlog.title: Tracing Hardware Design From Physical Devices to RTL (Infineon, TU Munich)
backlog.summary:
Researchers at Infineon Technologies and Technical University of Munich published a technical paper titled “From Physical Devices to RTL Models: Abstraction and Validation in Hardware Engineering.” Abstract: “This paper introduces the foundational principles underlying hardware engineering models and argues that abstraction is their defining characteristic. Because abstraction necessarily omits detail and constrains what engineers can... » read more
The post Tracing Hardware Design From Physical Devices to RTL (Infineon, TU Munich) appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.
bullets: Researchers from Infineon and TU Munich argue that abstraction is the defining characteristic of hardware engineering models, enabling complexity management at the cost of inherent incompleteness.

The paper categorizes design disciplines into lumped, value-discrete, and time-discrete models to explain how engineers bridge the gap between physical devices and register-transfer level (RTL) representations.
By formalizing the relationship between pre-clustered elements like transistors and gates, the authors provide a framework to improve design productivity and validation efficiency.

The approach uses what we believe... » read more
The post Ultra-Compact Photonic Bends Reduce Loss While Meeting Foundry Rules (Georgia Tech) appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.
bullets: Georgia Tech researchers developed a methodology for high-performance photonic waveguide bends with a compact 2.3 µm radius.

This approach improves fabrication tolerance, addressing a key bottleneck in the commercial viability of ultra-compact integrated photonic circuits.
